records.body:
Whole concept of built-in `poolOptions` was removed in
- https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest/pull/8705

We were planning that change over a year - pushing it later and later due to the complexity. I've written some of this reasoning in the PR:

> Vitest uses [`tinypool`](https://github.com/tinylibs/tinypool) for orchestrating how test files are run. Originally Tinypool was a fork of [`piscina`](https://github.com/piscinajs/piscina) which implemented `node:worker_threads` pooling only. Codebase of Piscina is very complex. It has features Vitest users do not need or cannot even use. When ever we add new features to Tinypool, we need to make sure we don't break those unused features that some other dependent package might be using.
> 
> Tinypool has some flaws that are making it hard to use in Vitest. When user is running Vitest workspaces with multiple pools, we easily end up in a situation where we allocate too many resources at the same time. For example in a 4 core CPU we may end up spinning 4 threads AND 4 processes at the same time. This is twice the amount of resources we intended to use. Tinypool does not support splitting resourceses across `runtime`. Also mixing `isolate: false` with `isolate: true` is very complex from Vitest's point of view - and not supported properly at the moment.
> 
> Originally Tinypool did not support `node:child_process` runtime. That was added for Vitest in https://github.com/tinylibs/tinypool/pull/65. While this feature works fine, there's still some overhead that the original `node:worker_threads` runtime required. I think there's room for some optimization and performance gains. Note that adding this feature to Piscina's codebase was unnecessarily difficult.
> 
> For the past 1-2 years, whenever we've seen Tinypool related weird errors in Vitest I've thought about rewriting Tinypool completely. However Tinypool is nowadays used by large packages like `facebook/docusaurus`, `jest-light-runner` and `@user-25/core`. Rewriting Tinypool just for Vitest's needs might break other's use cases. It would also be better if we could make changes to Vitest's pool implementation quickly, without any major releases.
> 
> We should replace Tinypool usage in Vitest with a custom internal pool implementation that lives in Vitest monorepo.

Any suggestions how we could do better? This was introduced as breaking change so I'm a bit surprised of your tone. 🤷

records.body:
One regression worth flagging: this version of `rerunFailed` no longer respects the active `filenamePattern`.

The existing `rerunFiles` filters failed files against the active filename pattern (`packages/vitest/src/node/core.ts:1204-1207` on `main`):

```ts
if (this.filenamePattern) {
  const filteredFiles = await this.globTestSpecifications(this.filenamePattern)
  files = files.filter(file => filteredFiles.some(f => f.moduleId === file))
}
```

So if a user pressed `p` to scope to a subset and then pressed `f`, the rerun stayed within that subset. By bypassing `rerunFiles`, the new code path skips that filter and reruns every failed file regardless of the active filename pattern.

Re-applying the same filter inline before iterating `failedFiles` (a small `globTestSpecifications(this.filenamePattern)` + `Set.has` intersection) preserves the existing watch UX.

There's also a smaller workspace-mode subtlety: in a multi-project workspace where the same `filepath` belongs to several projects, `state.getFiles([filepath])` returns one `File` per project, and the flatMap unions failed test ids across them. Test ids include the project name in their hash (`generateFileHash` in `test-specification.ts`), so the project-A spec ends up filtered against the union of A+B ids — which still works for A's tests but means project B's spec is constructed with ids it can never match (everything skipped). Iterating per failed `File` and looking up the project via `getProjectByName(file.projectName || '')` keeps the test ids scoped to the right project.

@user-1  
I’d really appreciate your guidance on a few architectural decisions here, especially around typing and fixture composition.

1) Strict Type Safety & Generic Constraints

While implementing `mergeTests`, I initially tried constraining inputs as:

```ts
T extends readonly TestAPI<any>[]
````

However this fails because `TestAPI` is invariant in its generic parameter due to the `TestCollectorCallable` definition:

```ts
<ExtraContext extends C>(...)
```

This makes:

```ts
TestAPI<{ a: number }>
```

not assignable to:

```ts
TestAPI<any>
```

So constraining to `TestAPI<any>[]` rejects valid usage.

To work around this, I relaxed the constraint to:

```ts
T extends readonly unknown[]
```

and enforced type validity structurally via `ExtractTestContext<T>`.

This preserves full context inference for consumers while avoiding the invariance trap.

My question:

Would you prefer a stricter nominal constraint even if it requires internal casts, or is structural validation acceptable here given the variance characteristics of `TestAPI`?

---

2)  Context Extraction Strategy

I initially attempted:

```ts
T extends TestAPI<infer C> ? C : never
```

But this proved unreliable because `TestAPI` is a complex intersection type with overloaded call signatures. In many cases TypeScript collapsed inference to `unknown` or `never`

Instead, I switched to structural extraction based on `beforeEach`, since it is the canonical API that consumes the contextual type:

```ts
T extends { beforeEach: (fn: infer F, ...args: any) => any }
  ? F extends (context: infer C, ...args: any) => any
    ? C
    : never
  : never
```

This also correctly accounts for the actual listener signature:

```ts
(context, suite)
```

Structurally matching on `beforeEach` felt more stable than relying on `TestAPI<infer C>`.

Would you prefer:

Structural extraction (as implemented), or
A nominal extraction approach even if it’s slightly less inference-friendly?

---

3) Fixture Merging Strategy

I explored implementing a low-level `merge()` directly on `TestFixtures`.

However, that would:

Bypass the `.extend()` validation pipeline
Duplicate dependency/scope validation logic
Risk drifting from canonical fixture behavior

Instead, I:

1. Added `toUserFixtures()` to serialize definition-time registrations
2. Re-applied them using `.extend()`

This keeps all validation inside the existing extension mechanism and preserves immutability.

Would you consider this acceptable alignment with Vitest’s design, or would you prefer fixture merging to happen at the `TestFixtures` level instead?


I’m happy to adjust direction based on your preference

I spent some time digging into this and it looks like the corruption isn’t actually happening inside Vitest’s stack parser or reporters
By the time the error reaches parseErrorStacktrace, the filename is already coming through as repro-ð.test.ts.

From what i traced the issue seems to originate earlier in Vite’s module-runner when the base64 source map is decoded. It currently prefers atob if it exists, but in Node.js atob returns a Latin-1 binary string instead of proper UTF-8 text
That causes non-ASCII filenames (like 👍) to get misinterpreted during JSON.parse which then propagates into the stack trace

I tested forcing UTF-8 decoding with Buffer.from(str, "base64").toString("utf-8"), and the stack trace shows the correct filename again. Since the corruption happens before Vitest processes the stack i don’t think this can be fixed cleanly on the Vitest side without adding heuristics

records.body: `shouldSkipNpmPassthrough()` decides to bypass the npm passthrough solely based on `packageManager: pnpm@<major>` (plus a couple env vars), but it does not consider `manage-package-manager-versions=false` when it is set via .npmrc/config. In that situation pnpm v10 won't switch to v11 in `main()`, so these commands stop working (they no longer reach npm) and instead fall through to pnpm's “command not found” path. Consider only skipping the passthrough when version switching is actually enabled (e.g. by reading that specific config early, or otherwise falling back to npm passthrough when switching is disabled), and update the loop-avoidance comment accordingly (the env var already prevents `switchCliVersion` recursion).

### Why this slipped through the beta cycle

Worth calling out that this is a **latent packaging defect** — only strict, path-traversal-validating extractors flag it. Every other installer just writes the dangling symlinks to disk, where they sit unused (pnpm itself never traverses `dist/node_modules/.bin/*` at runtime).

| Installer | Behavior | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **system `tar -xz`** | ✅ extracts as dangling symlinks | No safety check |
| **`get.pnpm.io/install.sh`** | ✅ works | Plain `tar -xz` under the hood |
| **`npm i -g @user-1/exe`** | ✅ works | npm's tarball extractor doesn't validate symlink targets |
| **corepack** | ✅ works | Pulls from npm registry; same as above |
| **asdf / mise / volta / fnm** | ✅ works | Same lenient tar approach |
| **[hermit](https://github.com/cashapp/hermit)** | ❌ refuses to extract | Validates symlink targets via [`sanitizeSymlinkTarget`](https://github.com/cashapp/hermit/blob/main/archive/archive.go#L666-L686) for path-traversal protection |

So it's understandable nobody noticed during ~9 betas + 5 RCs — every common install path silently tolerated the broken links. Hermit happens to be the canary.

**Repro:** https://github.com/jokull/pnpm-gvs-repro — `pnpm install && cd packages/app && pnpm exec tsc --noEmit` (0 errors without GVS, 1 with GVS). Verified with store prune + fresh download.

Tested GVS on a 24-package production monorepo (Next.js, React Aria Components, motion, react-map-gl, DatoCMS). 302 type errors with GVS, 0 without. `packageExtensions` injecting `@user-30/react` into peer-dep-only packages reduces to 31, but the remaining errors are structurally unfixable from userland.

The root cause: in standard mode, `.pnpm/<depPath>/node_modules/` is a merged view containing the package's deps plus `@user-30/*` from the consumer's devDependencies. In GVS mode, each store entry's `node_modules/` only contains declared dependencies (`lockfileToDepGraph.ts:150-155`). TypeScript resolves realpaths into the store, then can't find consumer-provided `@user-30` as siblings.

For example, `react-map-gl` depends on `mapbox-gl`. The consumer provides `@user-30/mapbox-gl` as a devDependency. In standard mode, `@user-30/mapbox-gl` is a sibling in `.pnpm/react-map-gl@.../node_modules/`. In GVS mode, it's absent from the store entry — so `onClick`'s event param collapses to `any`.

PR #11119 looks like it addresses this by exposing hoisted aliases in GVS package directories.

Separate issue: GVS also breaks bin shims (they reference `.pnpm/<pkg>@<version>/` paths that don't exist). `@user-1/plugin-esm-node-path` fixes this.

records.body:
> @user-31 Answer this question:
> 
> I have noticed that this PR lack integration tests. I wonder if integration tests would be possible....

After a thorough search through Verdaccio's source code (both the `<email>` package in `node_modules` and the `verdaccio-htpasswd` auth plugin), **Verdaccio does not support OTP/2FA**. There is no OTP-related code in its publish endpoint, user authentication, or any other part of its codebase. Verdaccio is a lightweight private npm proxy and deliberately does not implement the OTP challenge flow that the real npmjs.org registry uses (i.e., the `www-authenticate: otp` header that triggers `EOTP` in `npm-registry-fetch`).

Since Verdaccio doesn't support OTP, `@user-1/registry-mock` does not need to be edited — the limitation is deeper, in the registry itself.

**Conclusion: integration tests via Verdaccio are not possible for OTP/webauth flows.**

The right approach is unit tests with dependency injection, similar to how `oidcAuthToken.test.ts`, `oidcIdToken.test.ts`, and `oidcProvenance.test.ts` are structured in this PR. To make `publishWithOtpHandling` properly unit-testable, the following would need to be injectable (currently hardcoded):

1. The `publish()` function from `libnpmpublish` — so tests can throw an `EOTP` error on demand
2. `process.stdin.isTTY` / `process.stdout.isTTY` — so tests can simulate TTY mode
3. `enquirer.prompt` — so tests can mock the OTP prompt input
4. `fetch` inside `pollWebAuthDone` — so tests can mock the `doneUrl` polling

Without those injections, the logic can only be exercised end-to-end against a real registry that actually challenges with OTP.

Problems & Recommendations (prioritized):

1) Prototype pollution risk in extended query parser (HIGH)
   - Location: lib/utils.js -> parseExtendedQueryString uses qs.parse(str, { allowPrototypes: true })
   - Risk: If an application configures Express to use the 'extended' query parser, untrusted query strings can lead to prototype pollution, enabling attackers to modify Object.prototype and potentially bypass checks or manipulate application behavior.
   - Recommendation: Change allowPrototypes to false and/or add a safe wrapper that rejects prototype keys (e.g., "__proto__", "constructor"), or ensure that the default remains 'simple'. Document the risk in security guidance.

2) X-Powered-By header enabled by default (MEDIUM)
   - Location: lib/application.js -> this.enable('x-powered-by') in defaultConfiguration
   - Risk: Reveals server fingerprinting information to attackers.
   - Recommendation: Disable X-Powered-By by default (this.disable('x-powered-by')) or at minimum document how to disable it in the README/secure deployment guides.

3) Dependency maintenance & ecosystem risk (MEDIUM)
   - Location: package.json and .github/dependabot.yml present
   - Risk: Vulnerabilities in dependencies (send, qs, mime-types, etc.) can affect security. Some dependencies handle critical tasks (file serving, query parsing).
   - Recommendation: Continue using Dependabot and add periodic security audits (npm audit, Snyk). Add CI checks for outdated deps and security fixes. Pin critical dependency versions or adopt minimum supported versions with patch windows.

4) Template engine execution risk (LOW-MEDIUM)
   - Location: lib/view.js (require(mod).__express) — template engines execute user-provided templates
   - Risk: Template engines may execute code depending on engine capabilities. Malicious templates or unsafe engine options could lead to remote code execution in extreme cases.
   - Recommendation: Document best practices for choosing template engines and discourage enabling unsafe engine features. Add guidance in the docs about avoiding untrusted templates.

5) Cookie signing guidance (LOW)
   - Location: lib/response.js uses cookie-signature.sign
   - Risk: If applications use signed cookies without strong secrets, cookie integrity can be compromised.
   - Recommendation: Document signing best practices and emphasize secret management for app authors.

6) Good controls observed
   - X-Content-Type-Options set to 'nosniff' in JSON/JSONP responses (lib/response.js)
   - No uses of eval/new Function/child_process/vm in core library (search showed occurrences only in tests), which reduces attack surface.

The root cause is clear — mutating `config` properties directly means the overrides were being applied to the shared config object rather than producing a new one for this specific hook invocation. records.body:
For anyone else who comes accrods this issue: It is most likely caused by duplicate copies of the react package in an App's dependencies. A component imports hooks from one React instance, but the app is rendered by another, so the hook dispatcher is null (hence useSyncExternalStore crashing).

How to fix / check:

* Make sure libraries list react / react-dom as peerDependencies, not dependencies

* If building a library, externalize React in Rollup/Vite
 
* If using vite, add `resolve.dedupe: ["react", "react-dom"]` in the vite config

* Verify there’s only one physical react in node_modules
 
* Investigate your dependency graph using commands such as `npm why react` and `npm ls react`

Works in dev, breaks in prod is a classic symptom of this, because dev builds often automatically aggressively dedupe dependencies.

This doesn't need a repro @user-5 

It's really a feature request that the default type definition of `error` returned by `useSWR` hook is typed as `unknown` instead of `any`.

The issue @user-27 is having is that he has a lint rule that prevents assigning a variable to `any`. His options are to `// eslint-disable-next-line`, cast `as unknown` or to provide the error type to his `useSWR` generic like so:

```
  useSWR<ResponseType, ErrorType>
```

I think a lot of people using this library don't actually check or care what _type_ of error is being returned, they're just checking if the error property is set at all. But because of that very common and very useful `no-unsafe-assignment` lint rule, you can't do:

`const { error } = useSWR()` because that is an unsafe assignment of `any`.

Long and short of this is: the library error type default should be changed from `any` to `unknown`. Sounds like a pretty big breaking change but frankly anyone ignoring `any`s in their typescript codebase are also probably ignoring unsafe operations on `unknown`.
